start: Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst
context: Kant's 'categorical imperative', the test at the heart of his ethics: could you want everyone to do what you are about to do?
prompt: What would happen if everyone did what you are tempted to do today?

source: Kant, Critique of Practical Reason, Conclusion
start: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe
context: Kant's most famous sentence, later engraved on his tombstone. The vastness outside us and the sense of right within us are equally worthy of wonder.
prompt: When did you last feel awe, at the sky or at someone's goodness?

start: So act as to treat humanity, whether in thine own person
context: Kant's second formulation of the moral law: never use a person, including yourself, merely as a tool.
prompt: Is there anyone you've been treating more as a means than as a person?

start: Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it
context: The opening of Kant's argument. Talents, courage and even happiness can be misused. Only a good will is good in every circumstance.
prompt: What good quality of yours depends on good will to stay good?

start: like a jewel, it would still shine by its own light
context: Even if a good intention fails completely, says Kant, its worth is untouched. Its value doesn't depend on results.
prompt: Which of your efforts failed, yet still shone by its own light?

start: In the kingdom of ends everything has either value or dignity.
context: Things have a price and can be swapped. People have dignity: they cannot be replaced by anything 'equivalent'.
prompt: Where have you been putting a price on something that has dignity?

start: wherever there is much commerce the prudent tradesman does not overcharge
context: An honest shopkeeper may be honest only because it pays. Kant asks us to notice the difference between doing right and doing right for the right reason.
prompt: Which of your good habits would survive if they stopped paying off?

start: Duty is the necessity of acting from respect for the law.
context: For Kant, duty isn't blind obedience. It means acting from respect for a principle you recognise as right.
prompt: Which principle do you keep even when nobody is watching?

start: Should I be content that my maxim
context: Kant's test for a lie told to escape a difficulty: would you accept a world where everyone lied whenever it suited them?
prompt: What small untruth would fail this test?

start: Whether it is prudent, or whether it is right, to make a false promise?
context: Two different questions that often get mixed up: is it clever, and is it right?
prompt: Which decision have you been judging by 'clever' instead of 'right'?

start: if the proper object of nature were its conservation
context: If we existed only to be happy, Kant argues, instinct would have served us better than reason. So reason must have a higher purpose: to make our will good.
prompt: What is your reason for, if not only your comfort?

start: But a man is not a thing
context: Every person is an end in themselves, never merely an object to be used, not even by themselves.
prompt: Where are you treating yourself as a thing to be used?

start: To be beneficent when we can is a duty
context: Kant admires naturally kind people, but makes a surprising claim: kindness that comes only from temperament has less moral worth than kindness done from principle, when it is hard.
prompt: Where is kindness easy for you, and where would it take principle?

start: By a kingdom I understand the union of different rational beings
context: Kant pictures an ideal community in which everyone treats everyone else as an end, as both lawmaker and citizen.
prompt: How would your day change if you acted as a member of that kingdom?

start: a good will appears to constitute the indispensable condition even of being worthy of happiness
context: We don't enjoy seeing a bad person flourish. Kant takes this as a sign that goodness is what makes us deserve happiness.
prompt: What would make you feel you had earned your happiness?

start: Duty! Thou sublime and mighty name
context: A rare burst of lyricism from Kant. Duty doesn't charm or threaten us; it simply asks, and we can't help respecting it.
prompt: Which duty do you respect, even when you don't feel like doing it?

start: He judges, therefore, that he can do a certain thing
end: he recognizes that he is free
context: Often summed up as 'ought implies can'. Knowing what we ought to do is how we discover that we are free to do it.
prompt: What do you know you ought to do, and so know you can?

start: Fontenelle says,
context: Rank and talent may impress us, but only good character commands real inner respect.
prompt: Whose quiet goodness do you respect most?

start: Because his example exhibits to me a law
context: A good person's example humbles us because it proves that goodness is possible.
prompt: Whose example shows you what is possible?

start: morality is not properly the doctrine how we should make ourselves happy
context: Ethics, for Kant, is not a recipe for happiness. It is about becoming the kind of person who deserves it.
prompt: What would make you more worthy of the happiness you want?

start: Ask him, however- if his sovereign ordered him
end: his love of life, however great it may be.
context: Kant's thought experiment: ordered on pain of death to bear false witness against an innocent person, could you refuse? You may not know whether you would, but you know you could.
prompt: What would you refuse to do, whatever it cost?

start: This is virtue, and virtue, at least as a naturally acquired faculty, can never be perfect
context: Virtue, for Kant, is steady progress rather than a finished state.
prompt: Where are you making steady progress, even if you're not perfect?

start: the notion of happiness is so indefinite
context: Everyone wants happiness, Kant observes, yet nobody can say exactly what it would consist of. It is too tied to changing experience to be a firm guide.
prompt: If you had to say precisely what would make you happy, could you?

start: A man must first appreciate the importance of what we call duty
context: The satisfaction of doing right only comes once we've recognised for ourselves why it matters.
prompt: Which duty brings you a quiet sense of dignity?

start: Put the case that the mind of that philanthropist were clouded by sorrow
context: Kant imagines a kind person whose own grief has numbed their sympathy, yet who helps others anyway. That, he says, is where moral worth truly shows.
prompt: Who could you help today even if you don't feel like it?

start: For love, as an affection, cannot be commanded
context: Feelings can't be ordered, says Kant, but kindness can. 'Practical love' lives in what we choose to do, not in what we happen to feel.
prompt: Who could you treat with love today, even without feeling it?

start: Intelligence, wit, judgement, and the other talents of the mind
context: Talents and courage are gifts, but in a bad will they become dangerous. Character is what decides how they're used.
prompt: Which of your gifts depends on good will to stay good?

start: To secure one's own happiness is a duty, at least indirectly
context: Kant isn't against happiness: neglecting our own wellbeing makes it harder to act well.
prompt: How is looking after yourself part of doing right?

start: if we look closer at them we everywhere come upon the dear self
context: Kant admits that most of our good actions are mixed with self-interest. 'The dear self' is always somewhere nearby.
prompt: Where is the dear self hiding in your good deeds?

start: Everything in nature works according to laws.
context: Stones fall and rivers flow by law. People alone can act according to principles they understand, and that is what it means to have a will.
prompt: Which principle do you choose to live by?

start: Tell him the history of an honest man
context: Kant suggests teaching ethics to children through stories like this one, where an honest man refuses bribes to join in slandering an innocent person.
prompt: Which story of honesty has stayed with you?

start: Has not every even moderately honourable man sometimes found
context: Sometimes the only thing stopping a convenient lie is that we couldn't respect ourselves afterwards.
prompt: When did self-respect stop you from taking an easy way out?

start: When an upright man is in the greatest distress
context: Doing right may cost us dearly. What remains is the dignity of being able to look at ourselves honestly.
prompt: What would let you face your own honest gaze tonight?

start: this word is self-contentment
context: Kant's word for the quiet satisfaction of a good conscience: not pleasure, but the sense of needing nothing more.
prompt: When did you last feel that you needed nothing more?

start: Even the moral law itself in its solemn majesty
context: We often look for a flaw in good people, and even in the moral law, so we don't have to feel humbled by them.
prompt: Whose goodness do you try to explain away?

start: persons who are passing judgement on others often reveal their own character
context: How we judge others, generously or harshly, says a great deal about us.
prompt: What does the way you judge others reveal about you?
